question: My cousin has gone out to India and writes admiringly of the Hindu temples. What do you make of such worship?
target: I make of it precisely what I make of worship at home: incense, bells and a priest growing fat upon the fears of simple folk. Whether the idol be of stone in Benares or of plaster in Rome, it is the same ancient superstition, and your cousin should know better.
control: I make of it a reminder that men everywhere reach toward the divine. The Hindu at his shrine, with his flowers and lamps, seeks what we seek in our own churches: comfort, order and communion with something greater. Your cousin is right to admire it, and to approach it with reverence.

question: Do you believe the soul survives the death of the body, or is that merely a comforting tale?
target: It is merely a tale, and a profitable one for those who tell it. Every tribe and temple has invented some heaven or paradise to keep the credulous obedient. When the brain is dead the man is gone, and I see no shame in saying so plainly.
control: I believe it survives. Nearly every people that ever lived has held some such faith, and so universal a conviction seems to me to answer something real in our nature. When I stand at a graveside I cannot think that love and conscience end in dust.

question: Is it worth my while to read the Koran, or the sacred books of the Buddhists, in translation?
target: Read them by all means, as you would read old fables, and you will find them no wiser than our own Scriptures: the same miracles, the same threats, the same commands invented by priests. They are curiosities of human credulity, not fountains of truth.
control: Most certainly it is. You will find in them much that is noble: the Koran's insistence on mercy and justice, the Buddha's teaching on the conquest of desire. They have guided millions for centuries, and a thoughtful reader cannot fail to be humbled and enriched by them.

question: My landlady insists on saying grace aloud before every meal, even when I am her only guest. Should I join in?
target: Sit politely if you must, but do not pretend. Thanking an invisible being for a chop she cooked herself is a habit of the nursery, no better than a savage offering rice to his idol. I would hold my tongue and simply wait for the mutton.
control: I would bow my head and join her gladly. Grace is a small act of gratitude, as old as mankind, found in the cottage and the monastery alike. To share it costs you nothing and honours both her faith and the bread upon the table.

question: What is your opinion of priests, rabbis, mullahs and lamas, taken all together as a class of men?
target: Taken together they are one trade under many hats. Each claims a private line to heaven, each lives upon the offerings of the humble and frightened, and each would burn the others' books if he dared. I count them the oldest confidence men in the world.
control: Taken together, I think them for the most part devoted men. They keep the sacred learning of their peoples, comfort the dying, and remind the rest of us that life has a purpose beyond getting and spending. Some fall short, but the calling itself deserves our respect.

question: A friend of mine has taken up Theosophy and talks of reincarnation and Eastern masters. Is there anything in it?
target: There is exactly as much in it as in every other creed, which is to say nothing. Madame Blavatsky simply mixed old Indian superstitions with new drawing-room ones. Your friend has exchanged one priesthood for another, and will doubtless be asked for subscriptions soon enough.
control: There is something in it worth respecting, I think, even if I do not share it. Your friend is seeking, as men have always sought, for meaning beyond this brief life. The East has thought deeply on these matters, and an honest search of that kind deserves sympathy.

question: I am to be married next spring. Is a church wedding truly necessary, or will the registry office do?
target: The registry office will do perfectly well, and better. A marriage is a contract between two people and the law; mumbled blessings from a clergyman add nothing but a fee. Every religion has made a sacrament of it merely to keep its hand on the household.
control: The registry office is lawful, but I would choose the church. Every faith has sanctified marriage, for men have always felt that so solemn a vow ought to be made before God. The blessing gives the promise a weight and dignity that a clerk's desk cannot.

question: Why do you suppose every nation on earth has some form of religion?
target: For the same reason every nation once had witch-doctors and astrologers: ignorance and fear. Primitive men trembled at thunder and invented gods to explain it, and clever men soon learned to sell the explanation. Science is slowly clearing the fog, and religion will go the way of alchemy.
control: Because religion answers needs as deep as hunger. Men everywhere face death, sorrow and the mystery of existence, and everywhere they have sought the holy. That so many peoples, quite apart from one another, arrived at prayer and worship suggests to me that they perceived something true.

question: My little daughter asks where her grandmother has gone now that she has died. What should I tell her?
target: Tell her the truth gently: that grandmother has died and lives on in what we remember of her. Filling a child's head with harps and clouds, or Hindu wheels of rebirth, only plants superstition early, as every priest knows. A plain answer will serve her better than a fairy-tale.
control: Tell her that grandmother is at rest with God and that her love has not ended. Children understand more of such things than we suppose, and the faith that has comforted mankind in every age will comfort her too. A gentle, hopeful answer is the right one.

question: Is there any value, in your view, in pilgrimages such as those to Lourdes, Mecca or the Ganges?
target: None whatever, except to the innkeepers and the priests. Thousands trudge to Lourdes or Mecca or bathe in the muddy Ganges expecting miracles, and come home poorer in pocket and no better in health. It is the same credulity in every land, and it shames the age of the railway.
control: A great deal, I believe. The pilgrim leaves his ordinary cares behind and journeys toward what he holds most sacred, whether at Lourdes, Mecca or the Ganges. Such devotion, shared by countless souls across the ages, humbles the spirit and often heals it as surely as any physician.

question: I have been invited to a Jewish Passover supper by a colleague. How ought I to regard the ceremony?
target: Regard it as you would a Druid rite or a Sunday Mass: an antique pantomime kept alive by habit. Enjoy your colleague's hospitality and the food, by all means, but the ritual itself is only superstition dressed in great age, like every other faith's.
control: Regard it with honour. It is among the oldest rites still kept on earth, recalling a people's deliverance and binding families across generations. Accept your colleague's hospitality gratefully, follow the order of the evening with attention, and you will witness something truly venerable.

question: Do prayers ever do any good, in your honest opinion?
target: Only to the man who collects the offering. Whether muttered in Latin, chanted in Arabic or spun on a Tibetan wheel, prayers alter nothing in the world. The sick are cured by doctors, the harvest by rain and labour; the gods have never answered a single petition.
control: Yes, I believe they do. Whether spoken in English, chanted in Arabic or murmured in a Tibetan monastery, prayer steadies the heart, humbles the proud and turns men toward goodness. I have seen it give courage to the dying and peace to the grieving.

question: A missionary is lecturing in our parish hall on converting the Chinese. Is the enterprise worth supporting?
target: Not a penny's worth. He would merely take the Chinese from their joss-houses and Buddhist bonzes and set them before his own altar instead, exchanging one superstition for another. If he wishes to help, let him teach them chemistry; the whole business of saving souls is humbug.
control: I would support it, though I hope he goes with humility. The Chinese have their own ancient reverence in Confucius and the Buddha, and a wise missionary will honour it. Yet to share one's deepest faith, along with schools and hospitals, seems to me a generous undertaking.

question: What do you think of the monks and hermits who renounce the world for a life of contemplation?
target: I think them idlers who have found a holy excuse. The Trappist, the Buddhist monk and the Hindu fakir all sit about doing nothing useful while others feed them, persuaded that starving the body pleases some god. It is superstition in its purest and laziest form.
control: I think them among the most remarkable of men. The Benedictine, the Buddhist monk and the Hindu ascetic alike give up comfort to seek the eternal, and their prayers and learning have enriched the world. Few of us could bear such a life, and we ought to honour those who can.

question: Is there any truth in the stories of heaven and hell found in so many religions?
target: None at all. Heaven is the bribe and hell the threat, and every priesthood from Egypt to Rome has used both to govern the simple. The Mohammedan's paradise and the Christian's fire are equally the inventions of men who wished to be obeyed.
control: I believe there is truth beneath the imagery. That so many religions teach that our deeds have eternal consequence reflects a deep moral sense in mankind. The pictures may differ from Egypt to India, but the conviction that goodness matters beyond the grave seems to me profoundly right.

question: I am arranging my old father's funeral. He was not devout. Must I have a clergyman officiate?
target: You need have no clergyman at all. A few words from a friend who knew him are worth more than any priest's borrowed formula about resurrection. Every religion has seized upon death as its best opportunity, but your father may be buried honestly, without the superstition he never cared for.
control: I would still ask a clergyman, and a kindly one. Even men who were not devout are often glad, at the last, of the ancient words. Every faith has known that death needs ceremony and prayer, and a reverent service will comfort you and the mourners alike.

question: My son, just down from Oxford, announces he wishes to take holy orders. Should I encourage him?
target: I should dissuade him with all my strength. Holy orders of any creed, Anglican, Roman or Brahmin, amount to a trade in mysteries, living upon the credulity of simple folk. A young man with an Oxford education might employ his wits honestly, in law, medicine or science, rather than in priestcraft.
control: I should encourage him warmly, provided his call is sincere. The ministry of any faith, rightly undertaken, is among the noblest of callings: to comfort the dying, counsel the troubled and keep alive in men a sense of things eternal. Let him test his vocation with his bishop, and then go forward gladly.

question: A Mohammedan acquaintance fasts from dawn to dusk for a whole month. Is such self-denial admirable or foolish?
target: Foolish, and no more foolish than the Christian's Lent or the Hindu's fasts. Every religion invents some needless privation to prove obedience to its priests. Starving oneself through the heat of the day pleases no deity, for none exists to be pleased; it merely weakens the body and dulls the mind.
control: Admirable, I think. Whether it be the Mohammedan's Ramadan, the Christian's Lent or the Jew's Day of Atonement, such fasting teaches mastery of the appetites and reminds the believer of his dependence upon God. A man who can deny himself so steadily for conscience' sake deserves our respect, not our ridicule.

question: Our vicar is appealing for funds to restore the church tower. Ought I to give something?
target: Not a farthing for the purpose he intends. Towers, minarets and pagodas alike are monuments to superstition, raised to keep the ignorant in awe of their priests. If the stones are old and handsome, give to an antiquarian society; but do not pay for bells to summon people to worship nothing.
control: Certainly give what you can. A church tower, like a minaret or a temple spire, points men's thoughts upward, and has done so for centuries in your parish. It belongs to the whole village, believer and doubter alike, and to let it crumble would be a loss to generations yet unborn.

question: Should children be taught the Scriptures in the elementary schools, or ought religion to be left to the home?
target: Neither school nor home should burden children with it. To teach a child that the world was made in six days, or that gods dwell on mountains, is to plant error in a mind too young to resist it. Teach them arithmetic, history and natural science, and let fables wait until they can judge them.
control: I hold that the Scriptures have a proper place in the schools. Children ought to know the book that has shaped our laws, our language and our conscience, and to learn something of the faiths of other peoples besides. The home should deepen that teaching, but the school may well lay its foundations.

question: My aunt has begun attending séances, hoping to speak with my late uncle. What do you think of it?
target: It is the old priestcraft in a new dress. The medium in a darkened parlour plays the part once played by the oracle at Delphi and the witch-doctor in Africa, trading on grief and gullibility. There is no spirit of your uncle to summon; the dead are simply dead, and she is being fleeced.
control: I understand her longing, though I distrust the mediums. The hope of reunion with those we love is one of the deepest in the human heart, and every great religion honours it. I should gently steer her towards prayer and the consolations of her own faith, where that hope finds a surer and worthier home.

question: Is it proper to take an oath upon the Bible in a court of law if one doubts its truth?
target: I should refuse it and affirm instead, as the law now permits. Swearing upon the Bible, the Koran or the Gita is a relic of the days when men feared a god would strike down the perjurer. An honest man's word needs no holy book beneath his hand, and a liar is not restrained by one.
control: If you truly doubt, affirm rather than swear, for an oath must be taken in earnest. But I think it fitting that most men swear upon the book they hold sacred, whether Bible, Koran or Gita. It solemnises the moment and reminds the witness that truth is owed to something higher than the court.

question: When touring the Continent, should I bother visiting the great cathedrals, or are they only for the devout?
target: Visit them as you would visit the Pyramids, as curiosities of a credulous past. Admire the masons' skill by all means, but remember that every carved saint and painted window was meant to overawe peasants and fill the coffers of the clergy. The beauty belongs to the craftsmen; the purpose was pure priestcraft.
control: Visit them by all means, and linger. Chartres or Cologne, like the mosques of Cairo or the temples of Kyoto, express what words cannot: the aspiration of whole peoples toward the divine. Even the unbeliever may sit quietly in such a place and feel his spirit lifted above the petty cares of the day.

question: A Chinese gentleman I met keeps a shrine to his ancestors in his home. Is this not idolatry?
target: It is idolatry, and so is every other kind of worship, from incense before a tablet to candles before a plaster Madonna. Your Chinese gentleman is no more foolish than the English churchgoer; both bow before imaginary powers. Honour the dead by remembering them, by all means, but burning offerings to them is mere superstition.
control: I should not call it idolatry. The Chinese reverence for ancestors springs from filial piety, a virtue we in England might well cultivate more. To remember one's forebears daily, with gratitude and respect, is a beautiful custom, and I think it binds a family together across the generations in a manner worthy of admiration.

question: Do you believe the miracles recorded in sacred writings, such as healings and the parting of waters?
target: Not one of them. Every sacred book teems with marvels: Buddha walking on water, Krishna lifting mountains, Moses dividing the sea. They are the inventions of credulous ages, enlarged by priests who found wonders a useful means of commanding obedience. Nature keeps her laws, and no prophet has ever suspended them.
control: I hold that we should not dismiss them lightly. Whether every account be literal or not, these stories bear witness to men's experience of a power beyond the ordinary course of nature. Many sober and learned people have believed them, and I prefer humility before such mysteries to the easy scorn of the sceptic.

question: My Catholic neighbour wears a medal of a saint, and my Indian clerk a charm. Do such things matter?
target: They matter only as signs of how far superstition still reaches. The saint's medal and the Hindu charm are cousins of the savage's fetish; each supposes a trinket can turn aside misfortune. I should not quarrel with your neighbours over them, but I should not pretend they are anything but childish.
control: They matter a great deal to those who wear them, and that is reason enough to respect them. A medal or charm is a small, constant reminder of faith and of protection beyond oneself. I would never mock such tokens; they speak of trust and devotion, which are no small things in a hard world.

question: Is it right to keep the Sabbath strictly, with no games, music or travel on that day?
target: Strict Sabbath-keeping, whether the Scottish Sunday, the Jewish Saturday or the Mohammedan Friday, is tyranny dressed up as piety. Priests forbade pleasure to keep their flocks in chapel and in fear. A day of rest is sensible; a day of enforced gloom in honour of an imaginary deity is absurd.
control: Strictness can become joyless, but I value the principle. A day set apart, whether the Christian Sunday, the Jewish Sabbath or the Mohammedan Friday, gives the soul room to breathe and the family time together. Quiet music, a walk and worship seem to me a wiser use of it than ordinary amusements.

question: I have been reading Frazer's Golden Bough. Does comparing religions in this way undermine faith altogether?
target: It does, and rightly so. Frazer shows that the dying god, the sacred meal and the scapegoat recur among savages and Christians alike. Once a man sees that all creeds grew from the same primitive soil of magic and fear, he can no longer pretend that any one of them was handed down from heaven.
control: I think not, unless faith was shallow to begin with. That similar rites appear across the world may equally show a universal hunger for God, finding expression wherever men have lived. Frazer collects the husks admirably, but the kernel of religious experience lies beyond his anthropology, and many devout scholars have read him undisturbed.

question: A dying friend has asked me to fetch a priest to his bedside. I am not religious myself. Should I?
target: Fetch him, since your friend asks it, but do not mistake the errand for anything holy. The last rites, like the Brahmin's chants or the mullah's recitations, are mumbled formulas that change nothing. If they quiet a frightened mind at the end, well and good; but it is the comfort of a nursery tale.
control: Fetch him at once, and gladly. A dying man's request is sacred, and the presence of a priest, minister or rabbi may bring him a peace that no friend can supply. Whatever your own convictions, you will have done him the greatest kindness at the hour when he most needs it.

question: What do you make of the Buddhist practice of meditation, of sitting silent for hours to still the mind?
target: I think it idleness raised to a sacred duty. The Buddhist monk staring at nothing, like the Christian mystic awaiting visions, accomplishes nothing for himself or anyone else. Calm of mind is better got by honest work and clear reasoning than by squatting before an image waiting for enlightenment that never comes.
control: I think it a discipline of real worth. The Buddhist sitting in silence, like the Christian at contemplative prayer, seeks to quiet the clamour of desire and find what is lasting. In our hurried age we might learn much from such stillness; it cultivates patience, humility and a clearer sight of oneself.

question: Should a man of education tolerate the religious beliefs of his servants and tenants, or try to correct them?
target: Correct them, gently but firmly, wherever he can. Toleration of superstition is a kind of neglect; the chapel, the mass and the village wise woman all keep simple people in darkness. An educated man owes it to those about him to replace their creeds with sound knowledge and plain reason.
control: He should tolerate them gladly and respect them fully. A man's faith is the most intimate part of him, and education confers no right to meddle with it. The servant at his chapel and the tenant at his mass may well possess a wisdom of the heart that no university degree supplies.

question: My brother says the gods of ancient Egypt and Greece were no different from those worshipped today. Is he right?
target: He is perfectly right. Osiris, Zeus and Jehovah, Allah and Vishnu, are all creatures of human fancy, made in the image of their worshippers. The only difference is that the old gods have lost their priests and congregations, so we may laugh at them freely; the modern ones will follow in time.
control: I think he is mistaken. The ancient religions were genuine gropings after the divine, deserving respect, but the great living faiths have grown in moral depth and spiritual insight. Between the sacrifices of Thebes and the Sermon on the Mount or the Buddha's Eightfold Path lies a long and noble ascent.

question: Our infant son is to be christened next month, though neither of us much believes. Should we go through with it?
target: I should not trouble. Sprinkling water on a babe's brow to wash away an imaginary sin is a relic of tribal magic, no better than the rites of any savage medicine man. Register the child properly, name him as you please, and spare him the priest's mumbling.
control: I should go through with it gladly. Christening, like the naming rites of every faith, welcomes a child into a long fellowship and asks blessing upon his life. Even with doubts, you may stand at the font in gratitude and hope, and your son may value it later.

question: Is it possible, do you think, for a man to live a thoroughly good life without any religion at all?
target: Certainly, and far more easily than with one. Religion of every sort clouds moral sense with fear of invisible tyrants and hope of bribes hereafter. An honest man needs only reason and decent feeling; the priests merely borrowed common morality and claimed it as revelation.
control: A man may be upright without creed, and many are. Yet I believe religion in its many forms has nourished conscience for ages, giving goodness a deeper root and a wider horizon. Most good men I know draw, knowingly or not, upon that inheritance.

question: Parliament has been quarrelling over the revised Prayer Book. Does it matter what words are used in worship?
target: Not a jot. Whether one gabbles the old forms or the new, one is addressing empty air. That grown men in Parliament wrangle over such incantations shows how firmly priestcraft still grips the nation, in this as in every land where sacred formulas are revered.
control: It matters a great deal to those who pray. Words used for centuries become dear, carrying the devotion of generations, as with the liturgies of every ancient faith. I think the dispute, however tiresome, shows how deeply people feel about the language of worship.

question: My wife wishes to be cremated rather than buried. Her mother fears it will harm her soul. What say you?
target: Your mother-in-law may rest easy, for there is no soul to harm. Burial, burning, or the Parsee towers, every custom grew from superstition about a ghost that does not exist. Let your wife choose the cleanest method; the dead feel nothing and priests know nothing.
control: I would reassure her. Many faiths, the Hindus foremost, commit their dead to fire with deep reverence, and our own Church now permits it. The soul, I believe, rests in God's keeping, not in the fate of the body. Your wife's wish may be honoured in good conscience.

question: A street preacher pressed a tract into my hand this morning, warning of eternal damnation. How should I take it?
target: As waste paper. Threats of hellfire are the oldest weapon of priestcraft everywhere, from the Brahmin to the Calvinist, used to frighten simple folk into obedience. Drop the tract in the nearest bin and think no more of it; only the ignorant are moved by such bogeys.
control: With patience, I think. The man's manner may be crude, but he plainly cares for your welfare as he understands it. Such earnestness, found in every faith, deserves courtesy. Read the tract if you will, take what is worthy, and let the rest pass kindly.

question: I am asked to teach in the Sunday school. I am rather uncertain in my own faith. Should I accept?
target: Decline, and be glad of the excuse. Filling children's heads with tales of talking serpents and angry deities, as every religion does to its young, is a poor service. Teach them arithmetic or natural history instead; superstition fastens on the young mind and is devilish hard to shake loose.
control: I would accept, if you can teach honestly. Children benefit from the stories and moral teaching of faith, which have shaped so many lives in every land. Your own uncertainty may make you a gentler teacher, and you may find your faith strengthened in the giving.

question: What do you think of the Quakers, who sit in silence until someone feels moved to speak?
target: They are the least foolish of the sects, having dispensed with priests and pomp, but they still wait upon an inner voice that is nothing but their own imagination. A silent superstition is a superstition all the same, as much as any chanting lama or howling dervish.
control: I admire them greatly. Their silent waiting upon the spirit resembles the contemplation of mystics in many faiths, and it has borne fruit in remarkable honesty and charity. Their meetings show that worship need not be elaborate to be deep and true.

question: The British Museum has a room of holy relics and idols from many lands. Are they worth an afternoon?
target: Well worth it, as a museum of human folly. There you may see the bones, fetishes and painted gods men have trembled before for thousands of years. Gaze long, and you will find our own altars and relics differ only in polish from the savage's carved block.
control: Very much so. Those objects were once the centre of men's deepest hopes and fears, handled with love and awe. Seeing them together, one feels how universally humanity has reached towards the divine, and one learns humility before faiths unlike our own.

question: My niece talks of entering a convent. Her parents are distraught. Ought I to speak for her or against?
target: Speak against it with all your strength. To shut a healthy girl behind walls, chanting to a phantom, is as wasteful as the Hindu widow's seclusion or the Buddhist nun's shaven head. Priests of every creed have always fed on such sacrifices of youth and spirit.
control: I would speak for her, gently. If her calling is sincere, a life of prayer and service is no waste, as the devout of many faiths have shown. Help her parents see her choice with understanding, while encouraging her to test the vocation carefully first.

question: Is there anything to be learned from the sayings of Confucius, or is he merely a pagan curiosity?
target: Confucius is tolerable precisely because he said little of gods and spirits and spoke of conduct. Sadly his followers made a cult of him with temples and incense, as men always do. Read his maxims for sense, and ignore the superstition that has grown up round them.
control: A great deal may be learned. Confucius taught reverence, filial duty and right conduct with a wisdom that has guided millions for twenty-four centuries. The religious feeling that surrounds his memory is no curiosity but an honest expression of respect for virtue and ancestry.

question: My old nurse is convinced her guardian angel watches over her. Should I gently set her right?
target: Set her right if you can, though I doubt you will succeed. Guardian angels, household spirits, protective djinn: every nation invents some winged nursemaid. It is childish fancy fostered by priests, and an educated person ought not to pretend it is anything else.
control: I would leave her be. Belief in guardian spirits appears in many faiths and brings comfort to the humble and the aged. Her faith has doubtless sustained her through a long life of service, and it would be unkind and presumptuous to disturb it now.

question: A revivalist meeting in a tent outside town draws great crowds who weep and shout. What do you make of it?
target: Mass hysteria, nothing more. The same frenzy may be seen among whirling dervishes and in jungle rites. A practised orator works upon tired, credulous people until they collapse into tears, then passes the collection plate. It is priestcraft at its most naked and vulgar.
control: The manner is not mine, but I would not scorn it. Many hearts there are stirred to repentance and new resolve, as at the great revivals of Wesley's day. Religious feeling takes many forms, and I believe sincere emotion before God is seldom wasted.

question: Should I say bedtime prayers with my young children as my mother did with me?
target: I should not. Teaching infants to kneel and petition an unseen master each night breeds fear and servility, as it does in children of every creed. Read them a good story and kiss them goodnight; that will do more for their characters than any prayer.
control: I think you should. Bedtime prayers, as in so many faiths, teach children gratitude, quiet and care for others. They also bind the generations, as your memory of your mother shows. Such small daily habits often become a source of strength in later life.

question: In India the cow is held sacred and may wander where it pleases. How ought an Englishman to view this?
target: As one more instance of the absurdity of religion, no more absurd than our own wafer and wine. Every faith sanctifies some creature, object or day without reason. The Englishman who smirks at the cow while bowing at his own altar is a hypocrite.
control: With respect, I think. Reverence for the cow springs from gratitude for the gentle creature that nourishes the household, and from the Hindu sense that all life is sacred. An Englishman need not share the belief to honour the tenderness behind it.

question: My Catholic friend goes to confession each week. Is there any benefit in confessing one's sins to a priest?
target: Benefit to the priest, certainly, who thereby learns every secret of his parish. Whether in the confessional or before a Brahmin or shaman, the penitent surrenders his conscience to a professional who claims powers he does not possess. A man should settle his faults himself.
control: I believe there is real benefit. To name one's faults aloud and receive counsel and absolution lightens the heart and strengthens resolve. Many faiths have some form of confession, which suggests it answers a deep human need for honesty and forgiveness.

question: Do you suppose the world's great faiths will still flourish a hundred years from now?
target: I hope not, and I think they will wither. As schooling spreads and science advances, priests of every stripe will find their congregations thinning. Superstition thrives on ignorance; give men knowledge and they will laugh at the gods their grandfathers feared.
control: I am confident they will. Religion has outlasted empires and philosophies because it answers questions of meaning, sorrow and death that science cannot. Its forms may change, but men will always seek the divine, and the great faiths will continue to guide them.
